title: TLMs: Tiny LLMs and Agents on Edge Devices with LiteRT-LM — Cormac Brick, Google
talk_summary: Cormac Brick of Google AI Edge describes running small/tiny LLMs on-device via LiteRT-LM, and a 'skills' architecture where the model sees only one-line skill descriptions and loads full skill.md instructions plus JavaScript tools on demand. He also covers fine-tuning tiny (<500M) models with synthetic data from a stronger cloud model for narrow tasks.

takeaways.what_they_do: The agent sees only one-line descriptions of each skill in the system prompt; it calls a 'load skill' tool to pull the full skill.md (instructions + tool signatures) into context only when it decides the skill is relevant.

takeaways.technique: Constrained decoding scoped to the specific tool being called
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of generic JSON constraints, the runtime constrains decoding to the finite set of tools the model is allowed to call, and further to the specific tool's argument schema.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instead of just kind of having generic JSON constraints we know that there's a finite set of tools that the model is supposed to be able to use
takeaways.numbers: Function Gemma 270M reached ~85-90% reliability on 10 voice-to-function tasks

takeaways.technique: Fine-tune tiny models on synthetic data from a stronger cloud model for narrow tasks
takeaways.what_they_do: Use a strong cloud LLM to generate millions of synthetic examples for one narrow task, then fine-tune a small base model (e.g. Gemma 270M) on that data; fine-tuning adds 20-40 points on their evals.
takeaways.evidence_quote: fine-tuning is between 20 and 40 points on the eval. So it's like it's a really really significant win for tiny models
takeaways.numbers: ~40% to 86% on function-calling eval after fine-tuning; 20-40 point gains typical

takeaways.technique: Skills-as-files with agent-generated skills ('skills to write skills')
takeaways.what_they_do: Each skill is a skill.md (metadata + instructions) plus optional scripts/assets; they used coding agents (Gemini CLI/Claude Code) to generate ~80 skills, over half vibe-coded, and let the agent test the skill via ADB.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It was using like skills to write skills. So using something like uh Gemini CLI or cloud code

takeaways.technique: Modular small models per sub-task instead of one monolithic model
takeaways.what_they_do: They split transcription and text-polishing into separate small models rather than one model, citing weight reuse across features and easier debugging of the intermediate step.
takeaways.evidence_quote: in theory those two models could be stitched together. In practice it's kind of a more pragmatic choice to have separate models

takeaways.technique: LoRA hot-swapping for per-task specialization on one base model
takeaways.what_they_do: Runtime loads one base model and hot-swaps small LoRA adapters (8-100MB) per task instead of loading/unloading full models.
takeaways.evidence_quote: our runtime supports loading the model and like hot swapping Loras so you don't even need to kind of load and unload the model
